title: A Preregistered, Artifact‑Backed Paired Evaluation of a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (GVR‑ProtocolEval‑2026‑PR1) that compared LLM‑only configuration generation to a guarded generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline on 200 stratified intent→configuration NetOps tasks executed in a Dockerized Mininet emulator with a deterministic validator. Under the frozen preregistered contract we generated a single shared LLM candidate per task (generation_semantics="shared_initial_candidate") and scored it under both arms. All confirmatory episodes were verifier‑accepted: baseline 200/200, guarded 200/200 (n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). Paired difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729); exact paired McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. This outcome is a direct consequence of the executed shared‑candidate boundary (no repair attempts in confirmatory episodes) and therefore documents a preregistered boundary condition rather than measuring active repair efficacy. We publish the complete preregistration (SHA‑256 d913b4167cc6aa85b283e0703e0bfff0c3e8864405f5159d9a1a1cf5fc3fafdc), execution manifest and raw artifacts (execution/execution_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 d76af611272bd8e8b3a94290efecd6ecf634c5f3e36c2450c4245985e96931fb), representative scoring/validator traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 9235bce7875c1717dff5ac6be49c5769929b4e8509f5df404127efe9d6ee938f), model configuration (gpt-5-mini, execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820), and analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 7bc1bd2a42b5ac3f7adb61db47cf8dbe0472f678032abcd1e7c44f92ea2de71c) to permit deterministic reproduction and forensic follow‑ups. We explain why the confirmatory null arose, report preregistered power assumptions and the mismatch caused by baseline=100% acceptance, and specify precisely the minimal preregisterable follow‑ups required to evaluate repair value (independent per‑arm generation; enriched validator coverage).

sections.introduction: Automating natural‑language intent into device configurations is an operationally important NetOps capability but poses safety risks when generated configurations introduce reachability loss, policy violation, or service disruption. Architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair loops—generate→validate→repair (GVR)—are widely proposed as mitigations. Prior evaluations and benchmarks (NetConfEval, OpsEval, NetEval and others) have explored translation accuracy and model capability, but reproducible, preregistered paired tests that freeze generation, retry, and scoring semantics are rare. We preregistered and executed a deterministic, artifact‑archived paired experiment to measure whether a guarded GVR pipeline reduces operational failures relative to LLM‑only generation under a frozen contract; all artifacts needed to reproduce the run are archived with SHA‑256 manifests.
sections.related_work: Recent NetOps LLM and AIOps benchmark efforts evaluate intent‑to‑configuration translation, verifier‑assisted generation, and generation robustness (e.g., NetConfEval; OpsEval; NetEval). The generate–validate–repair design builds on generate‑and‑validate program repair and guarded execution literature in safety‑critical automation. Our contribution is not a new tool but a fully preregistered, deterministic paired execution with byte‑for‑byte archival of the preregistration, model calls, provider traces, validator traces, and scoring artifacts so the exact run (and its boundary condition) can be independently replayed and analysed.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. The study (GVR‑ProtocolEval‑2026‑PR1)was preregistered prior to execution; the immutable preregistration artifact SHA‑256 is d913b4167cc6aa85b283e0703e0bfff0c3e8864405f5159d9a1a1cf5fc3fafdc (archived). Primary estimand: paired difference in binary operational‑failure indicator (1 if deterministic validator reports reachability/policy failure; 0 otherwise). Design: stratified paired within‑task comparison on 200 confirmatory tasks (5 protocol families × 2 interaction modalities = 10 clusters; ≈20 tasks/cluster). Key frozen choices (published and enforced): model = gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...), generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (single LLM candidate per task shared across both arms to conserve model calls), maximum_model_calls = 400, retry policy restricted to infrastructure recovery. Execution harness and environment. Tasks were executed in a Dockerized Mininet emulator with a deterministic netops validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All model outputs, provider traces, validator runs, and scoring JSONs were archived and hashed (execution/execution_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 d76af611...). Scoring and inference. Primary inference used paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) plus the exact paired McNemar test as prespecified. Contamination controls and exclusions: automated token‑overlap detection against a curated vendor/RFC corpus was preregistered; items with ≥80% token overlap would be flagged and excluded from primary analysis; no confirmatory exclusions occurred (analysis/contamination_summary.csv archived).
sections.results: Execution summary and archival. Planned episodes = 400 (200 tasks × 2 arms). Completed episodes = 400; model calls used = 200 (one shared candidate per task per the preregistration). All raw artifacts and hashes are archived (execution/execution_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 d76af611...). Confirmatory outcomes. Scoring summary (analysis artifacts): baseline verifier‑accepted = 200/200; guarded verifier‑accepted = 200/200. Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 7bc1bd2a...) produced n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Primary inferential outputs: paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729); exact paired McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Representative artifact examples. We include three representative scored episodes that show full validator traces and hashes: task-000001 (responses and scoring JSON archived; response SHA‑256 f8de4d6e..., scoring JSON SHA‑256 9235bce7...), task-000002 (response SHA‑256 ae967f70..., scoring JSON SHA‑256 25e2c0c7...), task-000003 (response SHA‑256 f7f4db24..., scoring JSON SHA‑256 20e953b1...). Each scoring JSON contains the deterministic validator trace (parsed commands, required checks, final verdict) to support forensic inspection.
sections.discussion: Interpretation of the confirmatory null. The executed confirmatory boundary condition (shared_initial_candidate) was preregistered and enforced: a single LLM candidate per task was generated and then scored under both arms. As a result, repair_applied=false across confirmatory episodes and no repair‑driven divergence could occur; the run therefore documents that the shared single draw was verifier‑acceptable for all sampled tasks under the chosen validator and templates. This is a valid, fully reproducible boundary‑condition outcome, but it does not resolve whether active repair loops improve acceptance when repairs may alter candidates. Why baseline=100%? Three nonexclusive, artifact‑testable hypotheses exist (and we provide the archived evidence): (1) validator permissiveness or limited coverage: validator rule set exercised in scoring JSONs indicates the specific checks that fired (see execution/scoring/*.json SHA‑256 examples); (2) template solvability and model capability: archived shared candidates (execution/responses/*.txt and their hashes) match the validator's required command sequences for the synthetic templates; (3) potential training‑data overlap (memorization): automated contamination scans found no ≥80% token matches (analysis/contamination_summary.csv SHA‑256 389227f0...), but nondiscoverable pretraining overlap cannot be fully excluded. Power and preregistered assumptions. The preregistered power plan targeted a 10 percentage‑point absolute paired reduction at 80% power and assumed a nonzero baseline failure rate. Observed baseline success = 100% violates this assumption; consequently the preregistered MDE became unattainable in the executed run and the planned power does not apply. We therefore report exact observed counts and CIs and explicitly note that the original MDE target was not testable given observed data. Operational implications and required follow‑ups. To answer the original scientific question about repair efficacy, two minimal preregisterable changes are needed (both supported by and reproducible from the archived artifacts): (A) independent_generation_per_arm = true so that each arm receives an independent LLM draw (per‑arm generation), allowing repairs to be applied and exercised; (B) expand validator coverage and emulator fidelity (add timing, vendor‑syntax corner cases, and broader policy checks) and rerun the paired experiment with the larger validator rule set. The full artifact bundle already contains the deterministic harness, task bank, scoring pipeline, and code needed to run such follow‑ups deterministically (execution/*, analysis/*).
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed an autonomous paired study comparing LLM‑only generation and a guarded GVR pipeline across 200 stratified NetOps tasks under a frozen boundary in which one shared LLM candidate per task was generated and scored under both arms. Observed confirmatory outcomes were identical acceptance in both arms (n11=200), yielding a paired difference of 0.00 with a 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00] and McNemar p = 1.0. This null is a direct consequence of the executed shared‑candidate semantics and therefore documents a preregistered reproducible boundary condition rather than settling whether active repair loops improve operational acceptance. We publish the preregistration (SHA‑256 d913b416...), execution manifest and raw outputs (SHA‑256 d76af611...), model configuration (gpt‑5‑mini SHA‑256 a40e96e2...), representative scoring traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 9235bce7...), and analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 7bc1bd2a...) to enable deterministic replays and principled follow‑ups that modify generation semantics and validator coverage to evaluate repair value under realistic operational constraints.

limitations: Emulation and task scope: confirmatory bank used synthetic vendor‑like templates and a Dockerized Mininet emulator; production firmware/device heterogeneity and runtime complexity are not represented.

Single‑model, shared‑draw design: only gpt‑5‑mini was used and generation_semantics="shared_initial_candidate" produced a single LLM candidate per task so repair_attempts=0 for confirmatory episodes; thus the executed run did not exercise repair loops and cannot measure active repair efficacy.

Validator coverage: the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite rule set; untested operational properties (vendor firmware side effects, timing‑dependent behaviors) remain outside the measured construct.

Power‑plan mismatch: the preregistered power calculation assumed nonzero baseline failure rates; observed baseline success = 100% invalidates the preregistered MDE target and prevents demonstrating the originally planned effect size.

Contamination detection limits: automated token‑overlap checks flagged no confirmatory exclusions, but nondiscoverable overlap between model pretraining data and task templates cannot be fully excluded.
External generalizability: results under the executed boundary conditions do not generalize to other models, per‑arm sampling regimes, richer validators, or production heterogeneous device fleets.
